scenes.text: So, what are the SDGs, and why does health need education? You argued a version of this once, in Year 11. This time, three options. You have money to improve one community's health, and you can spend it on exactly one thing: a new clinic, a program that keeps students at school to the end of Year 12, or fixing the housing. Pick one. Then, what would you need to see in ten years to know you were right?

In Year 11 you saw the seventeen Sustainable Development Goals as a ring with health in the middle: adopted in 2015 with targets to 2030, universal, indivisible, comprehensive, and promising to leave no one behind. Here's the Year 12 step. Treat each feature as a design choice with a trade-off. Universal means Australia's own gaps count, like those by remoteness and for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples. Measurable, with targets and indicators, means progress can be checked, but only what's measured gets checked. And time-bound, but not legally binding, means almost every country signs up, because nobody can be forced, which is also the biggest weakness. For health, indivisibility matters most. Most of what decides health is decided outside the health system.

You met SDG 3's targets in Year 11: mothers and children surviving, infectious disease, early deaths from chronic disease and mental health, harm from alcohol, drugs and roads, and universal health coverage, everyone getting essential care without financial hardship. So here's where Australia stands. It does well on the first two. The live issues are chronic disease, mental health, and partial coverage. And notice something new. Most SDG 3 targets are outcomes, things that should be true, not actions. The actions are mostly found in the other goals.

SDG 4 is Quality Education: inclusive, fair education and lifelong learning for all, with equal access for girls, people with disability and Indigenous peoples. In Year 11 you traced how keeping girls at school saves children's lives. Here are the six routes underneath, and they show education is one of the strongest causes of health, not just as a stand-in for income. It builds health literacy, the skill to find and use health information. It leads to better, more secure work and income. It brings more control over your life, and low control means chronic stress. It changes what's affordable, available and normal, not because educated people are better. It makes it easier to navigate services. And it passes down. A mother's education is one of the strongest predictors of her children's survival and health, which is the Year 11 case. So education is a health intervention that works decades early, on several causes at once, and across generations.

And it runs both ways. Health also produces education. A child who's sick, hungry, or can't see or hear properly, or who's caring for a sick parent, doesn't attend or learn well. Untreated vision and hearing problems are among the most common, and most fixable, barriers to learning. So the two goals form a loop. Better child health means better learning, which means better work and health literacy, which means healthier adults, who raise healthier children. Run it the other way and it's a trap. Poor health interrupts school, which leads to insecure work and worse adult health. But you can intervene anywhere and turn the loop, like with vision and hearing checks or meals at school. That's why the other goals aren't background to health. They're the mechanism.

So what are the goals good for? They give health, education, housing and councils a shared language, which helps across the seams. They make it legitimate for a council fixing footpaths to call it health work. Their targets and group reporting make progress checkable. Then the limits. You know from Year 11 that they can't compel anyone, and countries report on themselves. Here are three more. Seventeen goals can scatter effort and let people report only what's going well. Some things are badly measured, especially for small groups. And signing up is cheap. The goals don't supply money, workers or political will. So the SDGs are a framework for thinking and reporting, not a program of work. In ten years, the evidence you'd want is outcomes by group, checked against the targets.
Two things to remember. Health and education are one loop. And outcomes sit in goal three, while the actions sit in the other goals.

Two exam questions. First. Action one: removing the cost barrier to essential medicines for concession card holders. Action two: free early childhood education in a low-income area. For each, say which goal it belongs to, SDG 3 or SDG 4, and the mechanism by which it improves health. Pause here to answer.

Action one is SDG 3, universal health coverage. People keep taking medicines for chronic conditions, so their disease stays controlled. Action two is SDG 4. It builds school readiness and later learning, which leads to work, income and health literacy, and it turns the loop early. The classic mistake is saying education doesn't affect health.

Second. In a town, many teenagers miss school to care for a parent with a chronic illness, and adult diabetes rates are high. Using the link between SDG 3 and SDG 4, explain how one action could improve both health and education. Pause here to answer.

One action is community nursing and carer support for the parents at home. Their diabetes is better controlled, which is an SDG 3 gain. Their teenagers are freed to attend and finish school, which is an SDG 4 gain. Over time, completion leads to better work and health literacy, so the loop turns the right way. The classic mistake is treating the two goals as separate problems.

So describe the features as fixes, name the targets in plain words, and show the loop in both directions. Now add two more goals that act on the same loop. Reduced inequalities, and sustainable cities and communities. How do fairer societies and better cities improve health?
